metadata.title: Trends in Children’s Reading Literacy Achievement 1991–2001
metadata.venue: International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement (IEA)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The Trends in IEA’s Reading Literacy Study used a two-stage stratified cluster sampling design (schools as the first stage; intact classrooms from the target grade as the second stage), implemented in parallel with PIRLS 2001 sampling. For the trend study, the school sample consisted of half of the PIRLS 2001 schools (every other school), and an additional classroom was sampled from the target grade within each selected school. The report indicates that each country was weighted to contribute equally to the overall mean and standard deviation of the IRT scale (common metric with mean 500, SD 100), and it also reports jackknife-based standard errors to reflect sampling uncertainty. The manuscript does not explicitly name the student weight variable(s) used in the international database, but it does state that sampling weights were computed by Statistics Canada and that weighted participation rates were produced; analysts should therefore apply the PIRLS/trend sampling weights when reproducing country estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This report is a trends/technical summary using PIRLS-style plausible-value technology for reading achievement, but it does not document a specific missing-data procedure for student questionnaire or achievement variables. Because the dependent outcomes are IRT-scaled reading achievement summaries derived via plausible values, the report focuses on scaling and sampling error estimation rather than detailing how missing questionnaire responses were handled. This omission is a reporting gap for missing-data handling details, which would be important for replication at the student-record level.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The target population was the grade containing the largest proportion of nine-year-olds (generally third or fourth grade). The trend study in 2001 re-administered the 1991 reading literacy test and used the 1991 student questionnaire items (student questionnaire administered in 2001). Sampling followed a two-stage stratified cluster design: schools were sampled first, then an intact classroom from the target grade within each sampled school. For the trend study, the school sample used half of the PIRLS 2001 schools (every other school) and sampled an additional classroom from the target grade for trend data collection. The report also notes within-sample exclusions and overall exclusions (e.g., school-level exclusions and within-sample exclusions), and it links questionnaire data to achievement data for analysis and reporting; however, it does not provide a full list of item-level or questionnaire-level missingness rules in the excerpted text.

data.outcome_summary: This IEA trends report summarizes changes in primary/elementary reading literacy achievement between 1991 and 2001 in nine countries (Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Italy, New Zealand, Singapore, Slovenia, Sweden, and the United States). Students were assessed in the grade containing the largest proportion of nine-year-olds (third or fourth grade) using the 1991 reading literacy test, covering three domains: narrative texts, expository texts, and documents. Achievement was placed on a common IRT scale across both time points (mean 500, SD 100), with four separate scales constructed (overall plus the three domains). To estimate uncertainty, the report uses jackknife procedures for sampling error and confidence intervals, and it applies plausible-value technology by generating five plausible values per student. The report also presents trends in selected home and school literacy activities from the 1991 student questionnaire administered again in 2001, but it does not fit predictive ML models; results are presented as descriptive trend comparisons with statistical significance indicators.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is a trends/assessment report rather than an empirical ML study. It does not train or evaluate machine-learning models on student-level predictors to predict a target variable; instead, it reports IRT-scaled achievement trends and questionnaire trend distributions. As a result, fields related to ML techniques, predictive targets, and structured ML findings are intentionally empty, while the methodological emphasis is on sampling design, IRT scaling, plausible values, and jackknife-based sampling error estimation.
